passage:
At the village temple festival, the drums were so loud Shankar could feel them in his teeth. He stood at the edge of the crowd with his cousin Lokesh, arms folded.
'You used to carry the lamp,' Lokesh said.
'I used to be terrified,' Shankar said. 'Remember Periyappa telling us that if we missed a single festival, the crops would fail and it would be our fault? I was nine. I lay awake over it.'
His voice came out sharper than he meant. A woman in front turned round.
'So now you're angry,' Lokesh said, not unkindly.
'Now I don't know what I am. Angry, mostly. Some days just empty.' Shankar watched the chariot lurch forward. 'Everyone expects me to either come back or announce I'm done. I can't do either yet.'
Lokesh handed him a cup of panakam and didn't argue.

qa.q: What did Periyappa say would happen if they missed a festival?
qa.a: He said the crops would fail and it would be their fault.

qa.q: What does Shankar's sharp voice reveal?
qa.a: It reveals anger at having been frightened as a child, still raw enough to spill out louder than he meant.

qa.q: Why is it wise that Shankar doesn't force a decision yet?
qa.a: Anger and emptiness are part of honest questioning; announcing a return or an exit just to end them wouldn't work, so giving himself time is more truthful.

qa.q: How does Lokesh respond to his cousin's anger?
qa.a: Lokesh listens without arguing and offers panakam, showing acceptance of Shankar's feelings without needing to share them.

grounding: It shows a young man angry at fear-based teaching and sometimes empty, refusing to rush into a firm conclusion.

passage:
The call to prayer drifted across the rooftops of Kadıköy as Zeynep sat on the balcony with cold tea. For most of her life that sound had meant something: stop, wash, turn toward something bigger. Now it only meant that it was evening.
She wasn't angry, the way some friends were about their upbringing. She just felt a quiet hollow where the meaning used to be, like a room after the furniture has gone.
Pablo, her flatmate, came out with a blanket. 'You've been out here an hour.'
'I keep waiting to feel something when I hear it,' she said. 'Either way. Relief, or missing it. Nothing comes.'
'Maybe it doesn't have to come yet,' Pablo said.
Zeynep pulled the blanket round her shoulders and listened to the last notes fade.

qa.q: How long had Zeynep been on the balcony, according to Pablo?
qa.a: Pablo says she had been out there an hour.

qa.q: What is Zeynep feeling as the call to prayer drifts over?
qa.a: She feels a quiet emptiness rather than anger, waiting for relief or longing that doesn't come.

qa.q: What does Pablo's reply offer Zeynep at this stage?
qa.a: By saying it doesn't have to come yet, Pablo gives her permission to stay with the emptiness without rushing to a conclusion.

qa.q: What might Pablo be noticing about Zeynep?
qa.a: Pablo notices she has sat alone for an hour and seems low, and chooses warmth and a blanket over advice.

grounding: It shows a young woman feeling a hollow quiet where religious meaning used to be, and being allowed not to rush to an answer.

passage:
Nandini tore out the page of her old school diary where she had copied prayers in her best handwriting. Her hands were shaking.
"Why are you so angry?" Yamini asked from the other bed in their Kolkata hostel room.
"Because they told me if I didn't fast, bad things would happen to Papa. I was eight! I fasted till I fainted once." Nandini crumpled the page. "And I believed every rule they gave me without a single question."
She had stopped believing a year ago, calmly, or so she'd thought. Now, suddenly, the anger had arrived, hot and bitter, about every fear she'd been handed as a child.
"Maybe you don't have to decide what you believe tonight," Yamini said.
"I just want to be done with it."
"I don't think it works that fast."
Nandini sat down, the crumpled page in her fist, and didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Nandini tear out of her old diary?
qa.a: The page where she had copied prayers in her best handwriting.

qa.q: Why is Nandini so angry now?
qa.a: She feels bitter and betrayed about the fears she was taught as a child, like fasting to protect Papa.

qa.q: What does Yamini's advice suggest about this stage?
qa.a: That anger is part of an honest process and rushing to a firm conclusion tonight won't end it; giving it time is wiser.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini to watch this?
qa.a: Yamini feels concerned and gentle, trying to steady her friend without taking sides.

grounding: A young woman who has stopped believing is suddenly flooded with anger at what she was taught, and her friend warns against rushing to a conclusion.

passage:
"You're up early," Francis said, finding Dhruv on the hostel balcony at 5 a.m.
"Habit. I used to do surya namaskar and prayers at this time. Every day since I was ten."
"And now?"
"Now I wake up and there's nothing to do with the time." Dhruv shrugged. "It's strange. I don't miss the rules. I don't think I believe any of it any more. But there's this quiet where it used to be."
"Like an empty room?"
"Exactly like that. Not sad, exactly. Just hollow."
"Have you told your parents?"
"What would I say? That I've figured it out? I haven't figured anything out. I just know the old answers stopped working."
Francis sat down beside him. "You don't have to fill the room today."
"Everyone online says just decide. Be an atheist, be a believer, pick a team."
"Do you want to pick a team?"
Dhruv watched the sky turn pink. "No. I want to sit here a bit longer."

qa.q: What did Dhruv use to do at 5 a.m.?
qa.a: Surya namaskar and prayers.

qa.q: What does Dhruv mean by 'this quiet where it used to be'?
qa.a: He feels a hollow emptiness, not quite sadness, where faith once gave shape and meaning to his mornings.

qa.q: Why is Francis's 'you don't have to fill the room today' good advice?
qa.a: It lets Dhruv stay honestly with the emptiness instead of rushing to pick a side, which wouldn't end the process anyway.

qa.q: What might Francis feel sitting beside Dhruv?
qa.a: Francis is likely calm and caring, content to keep a friend company rather than offer answers.

grounding: A young man who has lost his faith feels a hollow quiet where meaning used to sit, and resists pressure to rush to a firm conclusion.

passage:
The strangest part of losing my faith wasn't the arguments. It was Thursday evenings.
For twenty years, Thursday meant the Sai temple with my family: the bhajans, the prasad, my mother's hand on my back. Last year, after months of reading and questioning, I stopped believing. I thought I'd feel free. And I did, a little.
But on Thursday evenings now I sit in my flat in Hyderabad and feel hollow. Not sad. Just empty, like a house after the furniture's gone. Some weeks I'm angry instead, at how certain everyone was, at being told that doubt was a sin.
My sister Rashmi said, "Maybe you'll find something new." Friends online say, "Just commit to atheism." Both feel like being asked to buy new furniture before I've even swept the floor.
I'm Pradeep. I've decided the empty room can stay empty for a while.

qa.q: Which temple did Pradeep's family visit on Thursdays?
qa.a: The Sai temple.

qa.q: What does Pradeep feel on Thursday evenings now?
qa.a: Pradeep feels hollow and empty, sometimes angry, in the space where faith used to sit.

qa.q: What wise choice does Pradeep make about the empty room?
qa.a: To let it stay empty for a while instead of rushing to a firm new belief, accepting that the process takes time.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be hoping when she says Pradeep might find something new?
qa.a: Rashmi likely feels caring and a little worried, hoping her sibling won't stay in pain.

grounding: A young adult who has stopped believing feels hollow emptiness and flashes of anger, and refuses to rush to a new certainty.

passage:
Counsellor's note, university wellbeing centre, second session
Kavitha came in angry today. She said she spent her whole childhood being told that questioning was a sin, and now she feels "cheated" by years of rules she never chose. She tore a tissue into pieces while she spoke. Halfway through she went quiet and said the anger isn't the worst part. The worst part is the evenings, when the prayers used to be, and now there is "just nothing, a hollow space." Her friend Abhinav, she said, keeps telling her to decide once and for all, either go back or declare herself done. She asked me which one would make the feeling stop.
What I did next: I told her both the anger and the emptiness are common in this stage and are part of thinking honestly, and that no quick verdict is needed today. We agreed she will write for ten minutes each evening in that empty hour, and come back in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Kavitha tear into pieces while she spoke?
qa.a: She tore a tissue into pieces while she spoke.

qa.q: What two feelings does Kavitha describe?
qa.a: Kavitha feels angry and cheated about the rules she was raised with, and also a hollow emptiness in the evenings when the prayers used to be.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do well at this stage?
qa.a: The counsellor named both the anger and the emptiness as normal parts of honest questioning and did not push Kavitha to a quick decision, giving her a small evening routine instead.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's advice feel to Kavitha?
qa.a: Abhinav probably means well, but the push to decide once and for all may make Kavitha feel more pressured, as if the feelings are a problem to finish quickly.

grounding: Shows a young adult feeling both anger at what she was taught and a hollow quiet where meaning used to be, and being helped not to rush to a conclusion.
